title: The Korean church (1784)
hookLine: founded by laypeople who read Catholic books before any priest arrived

cards: Korean envoys come home from Beijing with books in their baggage. They're written in Chinese, the language of learning in Korea. Some are about the stars, some about mathematics.
And some are about a faith that calls God the Lord of Heaven, written by missionaries in China, among them Matteo Ricci, the Jesuit in a scholar's robe.
In Korea, a circle of scholars starts reading them, arguing about them, and slowly praying with them. There isn't a single priest in the country. Nobody has come to preach.

teach.b: First, faith by reading. These Korean scholars weren't converted by a missionary. They studied their way in, meeting to read, question and discuss.
Saint Paul wrote, in the Douay-Rheims: "Faith then cometh by hearing; and hearing by the word of Christ." Here, the hearing came through pages.
Second, a baptism in Beijing. They knew a Christian needs baptism, and had no one to give it.
So one of them, Yi Seung-hun, traveled with a diplomatic mission to Beijing, asked for baptism there, and received the name Peter. He came home and baptized his friends.

Third, a church with no clergy. Laypeople taught, gathered and led. Tradition says they even began appointing priests among themselves and celebrating sacraments, until they learned that only an ordained priest could.
They stopped, wrote to the bishop of Beijing, and asked him to send one. When a priest finally came in secret, he found a church already waiting.
The Korean government saw the new faith as a threat to the social order and to honoring ancestors, and waves of persecution followed.

Laypeople and priests died for it, among them Andrew Kim Taegon, a Korean priest, and Paul Chong Hasang, a layman who worked to bring priests into the country. The Church later declared them saints together.
In Korea, the faith wasn't carried in by clergy and handed down. Ordinary readers went looking for it, and then sent for a priest.

how: Korean Catholics honor their martyrs, lay and ordained, with shrines and pilgrimages, and the Church keeps a feast of Saints Andrew Kim Taegon, Paul Chong Hasang and companions.

games.q: you're one of the Korean scholars. you've read the books and want baptism, and there's no priest anywhere in the country. what do you do?
o: wait, and hope a priest comes someday.
send one of you to Beijing to be baptized, and bring it home.

games.why: Yi Seung-hun went with a diplomatic mission to Beijing, was baptized there as Peter, and came home to baptize his friends.

practice: Pick up whatever is close, a Gospel, a saint's life, a book of prayers, or the first page of Mark, and read a few lines, then stop and read them again.
Let one sentence stand out, the way a line caught those scholars, without trying to finish anything. If you pray, turn that sentence into a quiet conversation with God.

wordCard.voice: Yi Seung-hun. The Korean scholar who traveled to Beijing, asked for baptism, took the name Peter, and came home to baptize his friends.

orig.note: Korean: the teaching of the Lord of Heaven, the Korean name for the Catholic faith.

carryVoice: Your line: laypeople first. The week went from Alphonsus's mercy and Montfort's road, through Serra told honestly, the Jesuits restored, the Carmelites singing and a holy beggar, to readers in Korea. That's a week.
